_comment: Intrinsic efficacy at the mu-opioid receptor, relative to a full agonist, for the tolerance engine's occupancy-weighted drive (ToleranceStore's Stage 5c). Two rows, both from one paper and one assay, because that is all that can honestly be compared.
_what_this_is: The engine's quantity is how much tolerance one unit of receptor occupancy entrenches, relative to a full agonist, on (0, 1]. No laboratory measure IS that quantity. The closest available proxy is maximal receptor activation in an assay with as little signal amplification as possible, which is what these rows carry -- read that gap as real and do not present these as measured tolerance parameters.
_why_one_assay: Measured efficacy depends on receptor reserve and on how much the readout amplifies. The same compound spans a 7-fold range across assays: Bhowmik 2021 reports 7-hydroxymitragynine at Emax ~22% of DAMGO in the low-amplification Nb33 BRET assay and ~96% in the amplified cAMP CAMYEL assay, from one lab in one paper. A table mixing assays therefore encodes an ordering that is an artifact of methodology. Every row here must come from the Nb33 BRET assay, human receptor; a compound without an Nb33 number does not get a row, it gets the full-agonist default.
_not_bindings_relative_tau: This is deliberately NOT the `bindings.relative_tau` column, which is Black-Leff operational tau against DAMGO -- a different quantity on a different scale (buprenorphine 0.021 there). Wiring that column into the engine would rescale opioid tolerance drive roughly 24-fold for buprenorphine, and it carries no row for any Mitragyna alkaloid.

_withdrawn.mitragynine: Was 0.4 in Swift, uncited. Kruegel 2016 (pmid:27192616) measures Emax 34% of DAMGO at hMOR, but in the G-protein BRET assay -- not comparable to the Nb33 numbers below, and putting it beside them would recreate the mixed-assay ordering this file exists to avoid. Two further problems even within its own assay: Obeng 2021 (pmid:33384303) reads mitragynine as an ANTAGONIST at MOR in GTPgammaS, which Kruegel's own paper anticipates ('a low efficacy partial agonist in the brain may appear as an antagonist in the cell-based assays'); and a substantial share of what a mitragynine dose does in vivo is its metabolites, 7-hydroxymitragynine and, in humans specifically, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl -- so a parent-compound scalar is the wrong shape. Falls back to the full-agonist default, which overstates its entrenchment; that is a known cost, not an oversight.
_withdrawn.tianeptine: Was 0.5 in Swift with a comment calling it 'a low-efficacy mu-agonist'. That is wrong in direction, not just in magnitude. Gassaway 2014 (pmid:25026323), the paper that first identified tianeptine as a MOR agonist at all, characterizes it as an efficacious MOR agonist; Samuels 2017 (pmid:28303899) restates it as a full agonist; and Vandeputte 2020 (pmid:32734307) measures its efficacy as exceeding hydromorphone's by >=1.3-fold in beta-arrestin2 and >2.6-fold in mini-Gi. Only a receptor-depletion paradigm (Singleton 2024, pmid:39067665) reads it as partial, and that report gives no usable number. DO NOT reintroduce a low-efficacy value for tianeptine. The full-agonist default it now falls back to is closer to what is measured than the 0.5 ever was.

citation: Bhowmik S, Galeta J, Havel V, et al. Site selective C-H functionalization of Mitragyna alkaloids reveals a molecular switch for tuning opioid receptor signaling efficacy. Nat Commun. 2021;12:3858; doi:10.1038/s41467-021-23736-2
assay: Nb33 BRET, human mu-opioid receptor, maximal efficacy relative to DAMGO

substances.notes: Nb33 BRET at hMOR, Emax ~21% of DAMGO (~16% at mMOR). Stored as 0.20 rather than 0.21 deliberately: the paper writes both figures with a tilde and its discussion gives one number for this pair, 'the efficacy range comparable to buprenorphine (Emax ~ 20% versus DAMGO)'. Encoding 0.21 here and 0.22 for 7-hydroxymitragynine would manufacture an ordering the paper explicitly denies. Buprenorphine's efficacy is famously assay- and receptor-reserve-dependent -- in native guinea-pig tissue it reads as a pure functional antagonist (Romero 1999, pmid:10502307) and only shows partial agonism once receptors are overexpressed -- so never cite a number for it without naming the assay.

Nb33 BRET at hMOR, Emax ~22% of DAMGO (~14% at mMOR). The paper states the finding as an equivalence -- 7OH exhibits low 'intrinsic' efficacy 'comparable to that of buprenorphine' -- which is why both rows carry the same value. This corrects an ordering as well as a magnitude: the Swift table it replaces put 7-hydroxymitragynine at 0.6 ABOVE buprenorphine at 0.5, and the only assay designed to read intrinsic efficacy puts them level. Do not restore a value above buprenorphine's from an amplified assay; in the cAMP CAMYEL assay this same compound reads ~96%, and that number measures amplification, not the receptor.
